text:
1
Motivation
Many inputs are ordered (words, patches, frames). The goal is a contextual representation at
each position: the vector for token i should depend on the whole sequence (subject to masks),
not only on a local neighborhood.
Limits of earlier layers.
RNN / LSTM / GRU. State updates run left-to-right (or bidi-
rectionally with two passes). A long-range dependency must travel through many hops of the
recurrent chain; gradients and information both dilute. Training is hard to parallelize along the
sequence because step t waits on step t −1.
CNN. Convolution is parallel and local. Capturing wide context needs depth, large kernels,
or dilation. The inductive bias is strong for images with locality, weaker for arbitrary token–token
links in text.
Motivation.
We need a layer where every token can read every other token in one step (subject
to padding / causal masks), and where training can parallelize over positions.
What Transformer brings.
• Direct token–token interaction via attention (soft weighted mix of values).
• Parallel training over the sequence length n.
• One reusable block stacked L times (Encoder / causal block).
• Same core in language, vision (ViT patches), speech, multimodal — different tokenizers and
heads; same attention primitive.

Figure 1: RNN: many hops along the chain. Attention: direct soft links in one layer.
Cost trade-off (preview).
SDPA mixing is O(n2d); full MHA also has O(n d2) projections.
FFN is O(n d dff) — linear in n, wide in d. For long contexts, the quadratic term dominates
design choices (chunking, caching).
2
Application pipeline
Think of every application as the same skeleton: turn raw input into a sequence of vectors, run
a Transformer stack, aggregate (or decode), then a task head.

2.2
Tokenizer / front-end
For text: raw text →integer token ids of shape (B, n), together with a padding mask. Vocabulary
and special tokens must match the checkpoint. For vision or audio, the front-end may instead
produce continuous token vectors directly, such as patch embeddings or frame embeddings.
Watch-outs (text).
• Vocab mismatch ⇒silent garbage embeddings (ids look valid but mean something else).
• Casing / Unicode / whitespace changes ids.
• Pad id must match the attention mask; never let PAD attend as content.
• Truncation can cut the answer span in QA — check max length.

title: Common forms.
text:
Common forms.
• Learned lookup nn.Embedding (discrete tokens).
• Tied LM head: share input embedding with vocab projection (saves parameters; common in
LMs).
• Linear projection for continuous tokens / ViT patches.
• Position: absolute (sinusoidal / learned), relative bias, RoPE (rotary) — rotate Q, K by
position index.
2.4
Transformer (preview)
Stack of identical blocks; shape stays (B, n, d). Details: §§3–7.
2.5
Feature aggregation
Many tokens →a fixed summary for classification-style tasks:
• [CLS] token (BERT-style).
• Mean / max pool over non-pad tokens.
• Attention pool / learned query.
• Last token (common in causal LMs when encoding a prompt).
Autoregressive generation often has no separate pool: the LM head reads the last position each
step.
2.6
Task head and output
Linear / small MLP →class logits, token tags, span starts/ends, next-token vocab, . . . Same
stack; different head (+ decoding).
Two task patterns.
Encode once: classification / NLI / retrieval — one forward pass, then
a head on H. Autoregressive: next-token prediction with a causal mask — train in parallel
under the mask; generate sequentially at inference.
Both reuse the same attention formula; the mask and head change the behavior.
3
Inside the Transformer
Think of the Transformer as a feature transform block: L stacked Encoders map X0 to con-
textual H while keeping shape (B, n, d).
Hyperparameters at this level.
• B: batch size — sequences processed together
• n: sequence length — tokens per sequence (often padded)
• d: model width — embedding / hidden size
• L: depth — number of Encoder blocks
• h: heads — parallel attention patterns inside MHA
Tensor shape through the stack: (B, n, d). Print these shapes once before tuning hyperparameters
— most bugs are shape / mask bugs.
4

4
Encoder block
Shape preserved: X, Y ∈RB×n×d.
• LayerNorm: stabilize features (mean/var over the channel axis d, usually per token).
• MHA: mix across tokens (token mixing).
• FFN: transform each token independently (channel mixing).
• Circle + / skip: residual Y = X + F(X).
Residual and skip-link.
Y = X +F(X). The skip-link is a solid branch from the mid-arrow
out of X: a highway for identity features and gradients (Figure 9). Without residuals, deep stacks
of MHA+FFN are much harder to train.

Figure 7: Open one Encoder: one input X, one output Y ; residual add is a circle +; skip-links
split mid-arrow.
Pre-norm vs post-norm.
LN placement changes training dynamics.
• Pre-norm (LN before the sublayer): often easier for deep stacks; teaching default in modern
LMs.
• Post-norm (LN after residual add): original “Attention Is All You Need” layout.
Sketch (pre-norm):
Z = X + MHA(LN(X), M),
Y = Z + FFN(LN(Z)).
Common confusion.
Do not confuse the residual add with LayerNorm. Norm scales features;
the circle + merges the skip with the sublayer output.
5
Multi-head attention
MHA learns several soft routing patterns in parallel, then fuses them. Split into h heads: each
head has width dh = d/h.
One head learns one attention pattern; multiple heads can learn
different patterns in parallel (an intuition, not a guarantee of human-interpretable roles). After
SDPA, concat heads and Linear WO restore width d.

Why multiple heads?
One head = one attention matrix pattern (soft routing over keys).
Multiple heads share a fixed parameter budget (≈4d2 for WQ, WK, WV , WO, ignoring biases)

Implementation boundary.
WQ, WK, WV , WO live in MHA. SDPA consumes already-formed
Q, K, V and does not include those projections. When you say “attention,” check whether you
mean the full MHA block or only SDPA.
Parameter count (self-attention, no bias).
Four matrices of size d × d: about 4d2 weights.
Biases (if used) add 4d. Heads do not multiply this if you implement via a single d →d projection
then split.

(B, nq, dh). Concat over heads restores d.
• Self-attention: nq = nk = n; Q, K, V from the same X.
• Cross-attention: Q from one side (e.g. decoder), K, V from another (e.g. encoder) — same
formula.
Masks.
Add M before softmax. Typical values: 0 for allowed positions, −∞(or a large nega-
tive) for forbidden ones so softmax weight ≈0.
• Padding: hide PAD keys so content does not attend to pads.
• Causal: lower-triangular — position i cannot see j > i (GPT / decoder self-attention).
Never mask after softmax (that breaks the probability interpretation and is a common bug).
Cost.
n = sequence length, d = model width, dff = FFN hidden width. The SDPA mixing
cost is O(n2d). The full MHA block also includes O(n d2) linear projections for Q, K, V , and
the output projection — so roughly O(n d2 + n2d) in total. FFN: O(n d dff) (linear in n, wide in
d). For short n, FFN often dominates FLOPs; for long n, the quadratic attention term becomes
dominant.
Worked check (one query row).
Suppose scores after scale are [2.0, 0.0, −1.0] and no mask.
Softmax gives positive weights summing to 1; Y is that mixture of three value vectors. If the
third key is PAD, set M3 = −∞so its weight becomes 0 and the remaining two renormalize.

dff →d); MHA stays a closed box (Figure 18).

Continuous / patch tokens.
Flatten a patch (or a Mel frame, . . . ) and apply a linear map
to width d. ViT: image →non-overlapping patches →(B, n, d) after projection + position.
Position encodings (detail).
• Absolute learned: one vector per index 1..nmax; fails beyond training length unless extended.
• Sinusoidal: fixed frequencies; extrapolates more gracefully in theory.
• Relative / ALiBi / RoPE: encode pairwise or rotary position in attention scores — common
in modern LMs.
Padding and collation.
Batch variable-length sequences by padding to a common n. Always
pass the pad mask into attention; often also mask pad positions in the loss (ignore_index).

11.1
BERT (encoder-only)
BERT = Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Pretrained contextual text
encoder; use as a backbone (freeze or fine-tune) and attach a task head.
Topology.
X →Encoder stack →H. Every token sees left and right context. Strong for
understanding; not free-form generation.
Pretraining (MLM).
Mask random tokens; predict original ids. Forces deep bidirectional
features. SSL link: MLM = self-supervised objective; architecture = Transformer encoder (see
SSL chapter).
Downstream examples.
Text / sentiment classification; token tagging (NER, POS); span
extraction / QA; sentence similarity, NLI, retrieval. Aggregation: often [CLS] or mean pool over
tokens, then a linear head.
Pitfalls.
Tokenizer ̸= checkpoint; truncating the answer span in QA; forgetting to mask pads;
treating BERT as a generator.
11.2
GPT (decoder-only / causal)
GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Language model trained to predict the next token;
use as a generator (prompt →continue / chat / follow instructions).
Topology.
“Decoder-only” here means a causal Transformer stack without encoder cross-
attention:
xt ∼p(xt | x<t).
Each block is Encoder-like (LN, residual, FFN) but the mixer is Causal MHA = SDPA + causal
mask M so position i cannot see j > i.
Train vs infer.
Train: next-token CE in parallel over positions under the causal mask. Infer:
autoregressive decode — one token at a time until EOS / max length. SSL link: next-token
prediction = self-supervised objective; architecture = causal Transformer.
KV cache.
At step t, reuse past keys/values instead of recomputing attention over the whole
prefix from scratch. Essential for decode speed.
When to use.
Generation, chat, instruction following, in-context / few-shot prompting. Not
the first choice for pure encode-and-classify (BERT-like is simpler).
11.3
T5 (encoder–decoder)
T5 = Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer. Unify NLP tasks as text→text: prefix the task in the
input string; decode the answer as text.
14

title: Topology.
text:
Topology.
Bidirectional encoder over the input; causal decoder that cross-attends to encoder
states (Q from decoder, K, V from encoder).
Pretraining.
Span corruption: drop spans of tokens; decode the missing spans. Same SSL
spirit as masked LMs, with a seq2seq layout.
When to use.
Translation, summarization, structured generation conditioned on an input
document — any map from text to text.
11.4
ViT (vision as tokens)
ViT = Vision Transformer. Split the image into patches; project each patch to a token embed-
ding; run a BERT-like encoder; pool / CLS for classification.
Pipeline.
image →patches →(B, n, d) →encoders →(B, n, d) →pool →logits.
Same stack as Lecture 1; the novelty is the tokenizer (patches + position).
Vs CNN.
CNN: strong locality / translation bias, efficient on mid-size data.
ViT: global
attention from layer 1; often needs more data / stronger regularization; scales well with large
pretraining.
Choosing a family (rules of thumb).
• Understand / classify text →encoder (BERT-like).
• Free-form generate →decoder (GPT-like).
• Conditioned text map →T5-like.
• Images as patch tokens →ViT-style encoder.
12
Fine-tuning and efficiency
Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model with task data and a task head:
pretrained + task data + task head →adapted model.
Same adaptation idea as SSL: reuse a pretrained representation, then probe or fine-tune.
Contract.
Tokenizer ↔checkpoint ↔collate ↔head ↔loss ↔metric. These components
must remain consistent.
Workflow checklist.
1. Matching checkpoint + tokenizer / processor.
2. Task formulation / output format.
3. Dataset, split, collate, pad / truncate.
4. Head + loss + metrics.
5. Train, validate, save best, evaluate.
15

title: Modes.
text:
Modes.
Mode
Updates
When
Full FT
all weights
small models; max quality
Linear probe
head only
quick baseline; frozen backbone
LoRA / PEFT
low-rank adapters
large LMs; limited compute
Practical note: full FT a small Transformer you understand end-to-end first, before PEFT on a
huge checkpoint.
LoRA (idea).
Freeze pretrained W; learn a low-rank update ∆W = BA with r ≪min(size(W)).
Train few parameters; merge at deploy if desired.
Heads, pads, optimize.
Sequence / token / LM logits must match label shapes. Always mask
pads in attention (and often in the loss). AdamW; smaller LR for FT than from-scratch; warmup
on larger models.
Efficiency knobs.
Gradient accumulation (simulate larger batch); mixed precision; activation
checkpointing; watch sequence length (O(n2) attention).
Failure modes.
• Tokenizer / label / pad mismatch.
• Mask applied after softmax.
• LR too large; metric not aligned with the head.
Debugging tip: overfit one batch, then scale data / regularization.
13
Exercises and practice
1. Draw Pipeline →Stack →Encoder →MHA →SDPA from memory.
2. Derive shapes of Q, K, V, A, Y for one head and for MHA.
3. Explain why mask values are −∞before softmax.
4. Count MHA + FFN parameters for given d, h, dff (include biases).
5. Contrast padding vs causal on a toy n=4 matrix.
6. Practice: image →patches →encoder stack →pool →logits (small ViT-like classifier).
Optional baselines: Linear / MLP / CNN — same task, discuss inductive bias and cost.
Shape board (practice).
image →(B, n, din) →(B, n, d) →encoders →(B, n, d) →(B, C).
Print these shapes once before tuning.
What to analyze.
Accuracy vs #params / latency; does attention help vs CNN on this data
size? Failure cases; sensitivity to n / depth.

Debugging tip: overfit one batch, then scale data / regularization.
